new_statements.translation: The syllable consists of an initial, a rime and a tone. […] Tones: The Yi (Yiren) language has four tones, namely 55, 33, 31, 13.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote: line 21 reads exactly "[[音节]]由[[声母]]、[[韵母]]、[[声调]]组成。" and lines 29-30 read "=== 声调 ===" / "羿語有四個[[聲調]]，分別是55，33，31，13。" — verbatim as reported (the reader's "[…]" elides the 聲母/韵母 subsections, lines 23-27). The whole 語音 section (lines 20-30) is: syllable = initial + rime + tone; no consonant clusters, syllabic nasals; few rimes, no stop codas; four tones 55/33/31/13. No 重音/轻重/stress/accent string occurs anywhere in the held texts (grep over the two zh.wikipedia wikitexts, Hsiu 2013 slides text, en.wikipedia Gelao languages). The article's only reference is 張濟民 1993 仡佬語研究 (cited pp. 420-426 for vocabulary, p. 479 for the 1982 rescue recording of He Zixiu); last revised 2022-09-27 (re…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The language is tonal (four lexical tones on every syllable: high level 55, mid level 33, mid-falling 31, low-rising 13). No source examined says anything about word stress; the only data are a 1982 wordlist and a few sentences from a single elderly speaker, transcribed with tone digits only (Hsiu's spreadsheet of Zhang 1993 data confirms the 13/31/33/55 marking).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the Wikipedia text notes the data are limited and the speaker had not used the language for years, so forms may be unreliable.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone inventory stated for the syllable; corpus is citation-form wordlist material (pp. 420-426) plus simple sentences. Stress is not addressed at all, in any source found.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 'Gau' (gauu1234) = the language of the Yiren 羿人 (Chinese 羿语 Yiyu; autonym gau13, cf. Puding Xinzhai Gelao qau13), spoken until the 1980s at the Bijie (Guizhou) / Gulin (Sichuan) border; last speaker He Zixiu 何子秀 recorded in 1982. Hsiu (2013, 2019) classifies it as an extinct Red Gelao (A'ou) variety; Wikipedia files it as 'Qaw' under Gelao. Not to be confused with Qau/Gao (Central Gelao, gaoo1234/Ethnologue gqu) despite the similar name.
